sections.heading: Furnace and AC Trouble in Lincoln, and What Usually Causes It
body: Most no-heat and no-cooling calls trace back to a single part, not a dead system. These are the usual suspects.

items.title: The furnace clicks but never lights
items.text: Often a worn igniter or a dirty flame sensor. Both are small parts, and both are short repairs once the cause is confirmed.

items.title: The heat comes on, then shuts off
items.text: A clogged filter can make a furnace overheat and shut itself down. A flame sensor that can't prove the burner lit will do the same.

items.title: The air conditioner hums but won't start
items.text: A weak capacitor is a common cause, and it's one of the smaller repairs in the trade.

items.title: The vents blow air that isn't cold
items.text: Low refrigerant points to a leak, and ice on the line points to airflow. Adding refrigerant without finding the leak only delays the next call.

items.title: A heat pump that's stopped heating
items.text: Heat pumps heat and cool, so a failure shows up in both seasons. It's worth a call as soon as you notice it.

tail: If it's one of these, it's a repair. Whether the whole system is done is a separate question, and it comes second.

sections.heading: What Usually Goes Wrong With a Central Air Conditioner
body: A short list of parts accounts for most no-cooling calls. Ice on the refrigerant line, water around the indoor unit, an outdoor fan that isn't spinning or a breaker that trips each time it starts are all signs to stop and call.
If you see ice or water, turn the system off. A struggling air conditioner can turn a small repair into a bigger one.

items.title: A weak capacitor
items.text: It gives the compressor and the fan motor the jolt to start. When it fades, the unit hums and won't run. This is one of the most common repairs, and one of the less costly.

items.title: A frozen coil
items.text: A dirty filter or a blocked coil chokes the airflow until ice builds up. Thawing the coil is the easy part. The repair is finding out why it froze.

items.title: Low refrigerant
items.text: An air conditioner doesn't use refrigerant up, so low means a leak. Topping it off without fixing the leak buys a short break.

items.title: A fan or compressor motor on its way out
items.text: A slow or noisy motor is a warning. Replacing one early is a smaller job than replacing it after it quits.

items.title: A thermostat that isn't telling the unit to run
items.text: Dead batteries or a bad connection can look just like a failed air conditioner. It's worth ruling out.

sections.heading: Repair or Replace Your Air Conditioner?
body: Here's a rule you can check. If the problem is a capacitor, a motor or a coil that needs cleaning, repair is the answer, and it costs far less than a new system.
If the unit is old, repairs keep stacking up or the compressor has failed, that's when to price a new one. A large repair bill on an old unit is often money better put toward a replacement.
You'll hear which side you're on, including when the answer is to repair. When it's time to replace, we replace air conditioners and heat pumps, and we service all brands.

sections.heading: Four Quick Checks Before You Call
body: If you can do it safely, a few checks can save a visit, or at least give us more to go on when you call.
list: The thermostat: is it set to cool, and are the batteries fresh?
The breaker for the outdoor unit: has it tripped?
The filter: if it's gray and packed with dust, change it and give the system an hour.
The outdoor unit: clear away grass, leaves or anything stacked against it.

Your customers say the same things again and again: someone comes fast, finds the problem and explains it. Those words are on Google, not on your site, which has no customer reviews beyond one case study.

So this demo is for homeowners only: heating and cooling for the house, with AC repair on a page of its own. Your kitchen appliance work is real, and it deserves its own pages instead of sharing this one.
